speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The most recent amendments were by the Ministry of Transport (MOT).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2017, MOT introduced changes to the autonomous vehicle testing regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2018, the RTA was updated, along with the introduction of the Active Mobility Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) also amended the RTA in 2014 to make it an offence for motorists to hold any type of mobile communication device while driving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To make our roads safer, we need stronger deterrence against irresponsible driving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will do this by: (a) enhancing the criminal penalties for irresponsible driving; and (b) tightening the regulatory regime against irresponsible driving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will speak, first, on enhancing criminal penalties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Sun Xueling, who will be speaking in her Home Affairs capacity, will cover measures to tighten the regulatory regime, as well as other amendments for better road safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In recent years, the Traffic Police and the Land Transport Authority (LTA) have stepped up enforcement, education and engagement, to improve road safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Traffic Police have upgraded and expanded its enforcement camera network.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Earlier this year, the Traffic Police raised the composition sums for road traffic violations to ensure they remain effective deterrents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition, the Traffic Police and LTA ramped up public education and engagement, working with partners, such as the Singapore Road Safety Council.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are also fewer road traffic accidents resulting in injuries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also see more video footage of such behaviour being shared online.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Even if victims survive the accident, they, or their families, may suffer long-term problems – sometimes, medical; sometimes, permanent disabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In February 2016, a 62-year-old rag-and-bone lady was killed after a drink-driver rammed his vehicle into her.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The lady was the main caregiver to her nine-year-old grandson, who was suffering from a rare auto-immune condition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The driver had been drinking for nine straight hours before the accident.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Earlier this year, Staff Sgt Salinah, a Police Officer and young mother to three children, was knocked down at a pedestrian crossing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: After she was declared brain dead, her husband had to make the difficult decision to take her off life support.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Her husband said his children still miss their mother the most around bedtime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These are heart-wrenching tragedies that could have been avoided.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Enforcement, education and road safety infrastructure must certainly continue to be improved.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But we also need stronger deterrence against irresponsible driving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MHA reviewed the existing framework of criminal offences and penalties against irresponsible driving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In February this year, we announced our proposals and sought public feedback.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In particular, there was broad support for the enhanced penalties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also received suggestions, some of which have been adopted, and others which we intend to address.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will highlight these suggestions and clarifications in due course.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are three broad categories of changes: first, our overall approach in dealing with irresponsible driving offences, particularly those that result in accidents and hurt; second, enhancements to the criminal penalties for drink-driving and related offences; and third, the introduction of minimum mandatory sentences for the most egregious offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will start with our enhanced approach towards irresponsible driving offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, irresponsible driving offences are prosecuted in two ways.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One way is under the Penal Code, for Rash Act and Negligent Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Another way is under the RTA, for Reckless or Dangerous Driving, and Driving without Due Care or Reasonable Consideration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For better clarity and consistency, we propose to consolidate irresponsible driving offences under the RTA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also streamline the offences into two classes: the first category is Reckless or Dangerous Driving, which I will refer to as Dangerous Driving in the rest of the speech.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second category is Driving without Due Care or Reasonable Consideration, which I will refer to as Careless Driving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The definitions of Dangerous Driving and Careless Driving are currently in the RTA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Dangerous Driving is more serious than Careless Driving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The two can be differentiated, on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The three main considerations, among others, are as follows.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, whether the manner of driving predictably puts other road users at risk and cause other road users to be unable to react in time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Examples of driving that are considered as dangerous, as opposed to careless, include swerving across lanes suddenly and without warning, driving against the flow of traffic and speeding.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, whether the motorist had driven, even though he should have known he was not in a condition to drive safely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Examples of behaviour that are considered dangerous include using mobile devices while driving and failing to use visual aids, such as spectacles, even though he is seriously short-sighted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Third, whether the road situation required the motorist to take extra care but he did not.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Examples include when he is approaching a zebra crossing, or a junction where other road users have the right of way.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When determining the punishment, we will look at the circumstances under which the offence is committed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The threshold for Dangerous Driving is higher than Careless Driving; so, too, the penalties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Besides looking at the circumstances of the offence, our enhanced approach will also consider the level of harm caused.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such tiering of harm is not new in our laws.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To summarise, we will enhance our overall approach to penalise irresponsible driving depending on: (a) the circumstances of the offence, whether it constitutes Dangerous Driving or Careless Driving; and (b) the level of harm caused, whether they result in Death, Grievous Hurt, Hurt or Endangering Life.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, our penalties for irresponsible driving offences are generally less severe than in other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, for Dangerous Driving causing Death, the maximum jail term in Singapore is only five years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is 14 years in the United Kingdom (UK), 10 years in New South Wales in Australia, Hong Kong as well as Malaysia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In most instances, the actual sentences meted out are lower than the maximum penalties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In recent times, there were at least two separate instances of a motorist beating the red light, colliding into and killing another person.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the April 2017 case, a pedestrian was killed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the April 2018 case, the vehicle collided into another car, killing the rear passenger.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Both motorists were charged for the offence of Dangerous Driving causing Death.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Their sentences were five and seven months of imprisonment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also need to raise sentencing norms for egregious irresponsible driving offences, particularly those that result in death or some form of permanent disabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clauses 13 and 14 of the Bill amend sections 64 and 65 to introduce higher maximum jail terms and fines, where applicable, as compared to the existing penalties under the Penal Code and RTA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also introduce additional levers to take irresponsible motorists off the roads more quickly and for longer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, we will give Traffic Police the discretion to impose immediate suspension for all Dangerous Driving offences, as well as Careless Driving offences that cause Death or Grievous Hurt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Otherwise, these motorists can continue to drive until such time that they are convicted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Traffic Police already have the discretion to do so for offences that result in death, serious injury or serious damage to buildings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 11 amends section 47C to cover all cases of Dangerous Driving as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, we will introduce minimum disqualification (DQ) periods for offences that cause Death and Grievous Hurt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In exceptional circumstances, such as where the motorist committed the offence while rushing for a medical emergency, the Courts will have the discretion not to apply the minimum DQ periods.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clauses 13 and 14 of the Bill amend sections 64 and 65 for these purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Third, the Public Prosecutor may apply for forfeiture of a vehicle used for an expanded group of offences, such as Dangerous Driving causing Death or Grievous Hurt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clauses 3 and 15 bring this into effect.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For these offences, the Courts will have the discretion not to forfeit the vehicle if the offender is not the vehicle owner and had driven the vehicle without the owner’s consent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition, for specified offences, the Courts will also have the discretion not to forfeit the vehicle, if there are good reasons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For instance, if the motorist has committed the offence while rushing to the hospital for a medical emergency.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As we are consolidating irresponsible driving offences under RTA, we should make clear the understanding of "repeat offender".

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will include a person who has a previous conviction for any Rash or Negligent Act offence in the Penal Code where irresponsible driving was involved.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Likewise, any Dangerous Driving or Careless Driving convictions under RTA, or speeding-related convictions are included.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Speeding-related convictions will include offences, such as Illegal Speed Trials, colloquially known as illegal street racing, which have been tried and convicted by the Courts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, it will not include speeding-related offences which have been compounded, which is the way most minor speeding offences are settled today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Drivers who are drunk or drug-impaired show a blatant disregard for the safety of other road users.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are one of the biggest contributors to serious accidents on our roads.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These are also accidents that clearly could have been avoided if the motorist had not come under influence or did not drive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, such motorists typically face the same maximum penalties as other motorists who cause accidents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The judge may take into consideration that the offender was driving under influence during the sentencing itself.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But it would be clearer to have our intentions codified in law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, our intention is for offenders driving under influence to face stiffer penalties to signal the aggravated seriousness of their actions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In August 2013, a motorist drove his car at high speeds, swaying between lanes along the Central Expressway (CTE).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Eventually, he rammed into a group of five, killing four victims.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: He was sentenced to the maximum penalty of five years in jail for dangerous driving causing death, the maximum punishment available.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Court could not mete out higher penalties even though he had knowingly consumed drugs before driving and was a recalcitrant offender.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We, therefore, propose to introduce additional penalties for a motorist who commit a Dangerous Driving or Careless Driving offence, and who is found guilty for driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs; or had refused to take a breathalyser or blood alcohol test when directed by Traffic Police.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These will be in the form of additional maximum penalties and additional minimum DQ periods.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: An individual will be deemed a repeat offender for an offence of driving under influence if he has a previous conviction for driving under influence, for being in charge of a motor vehicle while under the influence of drugs or alcohol, or for failure to produce a specimen for a drug or alcohol test.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The consumption of alcohol or drugs already makes a motorist a danger to other road users.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Section 67 in clause 17 of the Bill will raise the penalties to about double the current levels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also raise the existing minimum DQ period to two years for first-time driving under influence offenders and five years for second-time driving under influence offenders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A lifelong disqualification will be imposed on third-time driving under influence offenders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition, we will amend section 47C through clause 11 to allow Traffic Police to impose immediate suspension for all driving under influence offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: How exactly then does MHA intend to raise the sentencing norms for irresponsible driving offences?

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is where the last category of changes come in.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will set benchmarks based on egregious offences where manifestly inadequate jail sentences must be avoided.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will introduce mandatory minimum jail sentences (MMS) for Dangerous Driving causing Death or Grievous Hurt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Repeat offenders will be jailed for at least four years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also have MMS for the offences of Dangerous Driving causing Death or Grievous Hurt, where driving under influence is involved.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A first-time offender who causes death will be jailed for at least three years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Repeat offenders can face minimum sentences of up to six years in jail.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Take, for example, the case of the 62-year-old rag-and-bone lady whom I mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The offender had been drinking for nine straight hours and was charged for the offence of causing death by a rash act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: During sentencing, also taken into consideration were one count of drink-driving and another count of causing grievous hurt to the dead victim’s husband by a rash act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In all, against a maximum penalty of five years’ imprisonment, he received a term of 10 months and disqualification of eight years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many people felt rightly that the motorist was let off too lightly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With the changes, the offender will be sentenced to at least three years in jail if he is convicted of both Dangerous Driving causing Death and driving under influence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The minimum disqualification will also be lengthened to 12 years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some respondents noted that while MMSes were justified for egregious offenders, there may be rare but valid cases where exceptional extenuating circumstances prevail and where imposing the minimum jail sentence may result in an unfair punishment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We need not prescribe the extenuating instances in law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Instead, we have introduced an amendment to the Bill to provide the Courts with discretion to deviate from and impose a sentence lower than the MMS terms should there be special reasons to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Special reasons must constitute exceptional mitigating factors or circumstances specific to the case.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, the offender was rushing to send a passenger for emergency medical treatment in a life-and-death situation when the accident occurred.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: During our public engagement, some respondents asked if punishments for inconsiderate non-motorists should also be increased.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The road situation today is more complex, compared to 20 years ago when the last major review was conducted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are new groups of road users, such as active mobility device users or new types of vocational drivers and riders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Motorists alone cannot be held responsible for the road safety of all road users.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These amendments, therefore, cannot be viewed in isolation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MHA has been working with our counterparts at MOT and the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) to address other aspects of road safety, such as active mobility and vocational drivers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As I mentioned earlier, the Traffic Police and LTA have taken steps beyond enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I will now be speaking in my capacity as Senior Parliamentary Secretary for MHA and explain the Ministry’s views on the remaining amendments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: First, I will cover the measures to tighten the regulatory regime against irresponsible driving; and second, other minor amendments to improve road safety.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Traffic Police operate the Driver Improvement Points System (DIPS).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Under this regime, a motorist clocks demerit points when he commits a traffic offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The more severe the offence, the more demerit points it will attract.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Motorists who exceed a stipulated threshold will have their licences suspended.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The DIPS regime is a deterrent against risk-taking behaviour that is dangerous to other road users, such as illegal U-turns, speeding and beating red-lights.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MHA intends to enhance the DIPS regime to further deter risk-taking behaviour by motorists.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I will cover each of the measures in turn.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: First, to streamline the suspension and revocation process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Currently, some errant motorists delay the suspension or revocation of their licences by misusing the appeals mechanism.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They file multiple unmerited appeals at different junctures and through different channels.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: By doing so, they drag out the process so that they can continue to drive in the interim.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But we need to remember, these are irresponsible drivers who have already been picked up for multiple offences leading to a suspension or revocation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Police, where possible, will process and respond to an appeal within two weeks of receiving the appeal.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, DCP will have the power to suspend or revoke the licence four weeks after the date of its notice, even if the appeal is still being processed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, there are cases where the motorist only submits an appeal close to four weeks after receiving the notice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The DCP may still suspend or revoke the licence first and subsequently rescind the suspension or revocation if there are valid grounds to do so.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We need to bear in mind that to be facing a suspension or revocation, the errant motorist will already have committed several offences prior.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: First, a suspension or revocation is imposed only when objective criteria are met.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For suspension, this usually happens when the motorist has breached the demerit point threshold of either 24 or 12 points, depending on how many prior suspensions he has had.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For revocation, this happens when he is on probation and has clocked more than 12 demerit points.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Second, for Traffic Police to mete out demerit points to a motorist, one of two conditions must apply.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: First, the Courts have convicted the motorist of the offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Or two, the motorist has compounded the offence he is reasonably suspected to have committed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This means that the motorist would have already had a previous opportunity to appeal against these individual offences, by either contesting it in Court or appealing to Traffic Police during an offer of composition, before the demerit points were awarded to him.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Third, motorists who are caught committing a road traffic violation also typically have little reason to dispute against the violation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Traffic Police only take enforcement action when there are strong grounds that an offence has been made out.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For the majority of offences, the evidence typically comes in the form of photographic or video evidence or by detection from Traffic Police’s enforcement unit.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I would also like to speak on appeals in general.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: A number of affected motorists appeal against suspension or revocation on the basis that they need to drive as part of their job.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Actually, if an individual depends on driving to make a living, that is all the more reason for him to drive safely and for him to be off the roads if he is unable or unwilling to do so.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Traffic Police, as part of the overall road safety strategy, offer motorists the opportunity to improve their driving behaviour through retraining courses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Upon completion of the course, motorists will have four demerit points expunged from their records.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To put this in perspective, the upper scale of the suspension applies to very serious serial offenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Those who are facing their seventh or more suspension will have their licence suspended for five years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As Members can see, these are recalcitrant offenders who are a real danger on the roads to themselves, to other motorists and road users.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: That there are drivers who have been slapped with six or more suspensions may sound unbelievable, but I assure you, it is not unheard of.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I now move to the third measure – revoking all of an individual's probationary licences, as long as any one of them is revoked.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At present, under certain circumstances, a motorist may continue to hold probationary licences for other vehicle classes even though one of his probationary licences has been revoked.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is a gap that should be addressed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Traffic Police expect a motorist to take extra care to drive safely when he is on probation, given his relative inexperience.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If he breaches the demerit point threshold for any of his probationary licences, for the safety of other road users, he should no longer be allowed to drive any vehicle for which he holds a probationary licence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: A person’s record of compounded offences is a useful indicator of his driving behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The first pertains to the definition of animals, and the obligations of motorists when accidents involving animals occur.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The current definition of animals, which is restricted to an exhaustive list of farm animals, such as cattle, horses and dogs, is archaic and not relevant to our context.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will remove this definition, and instead will rely on the general definition of the word.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Motorists will be obliged to stop their vehicle, only if it is safe to do so, and render any necessary assistance in accidents involving animals in two scenarios.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: First, if the body of the animal or carcass is a road safety hazard, motorists should take steps to alert other road users to the obstruction.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, in road accidents involving wild boars, the carcass is likely to result in some obstruction to vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Second, if there is reasonable belief that the animal may have an owner, motorists should make attempts to inform the owner or the Police, for example, in road accidents involving dogs that are wearing a collar.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Today, Traffic Police no longer rely on physical licences to ascertain an individual's driving qualifications.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Traffic Police can access this information backend, using an individual's National Registration Identity Card and date of birth.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Therefore, as part of the effort towards digitisation, TP plan to issue physical driving licences to motorists only upon request.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Hence, we will amend RTA to remove existing requirements for individuals to surrender their physical licences, if they do not have one.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The third amendment pertains to the penalties for riding without a helmet.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At present, section 74 of the RTA subjects motorcyclists and pillion riders who do not wear helmets to a fine of up to $200.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This Bill will make our roads safer, by increasing deterrence against irresponsible driving.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the road is shared among many users and road conditions are dynamic.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Dangerous or careless driving puts the driver's own life at risk and pedestrians crossing the road or walking on the pavement at risk.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Their actions leave a lasting impact on the victims' lives, their families and even sometimes their own lives.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In May 2018, a driver looked down briefly, veered towards the right, mounted a kerb, colliding into the centre median, a sign and a couple of railings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The accident left his passenger tetraplegic and bedbound, a condition likely to be permanent.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In June 2018, while enroute home to Singapore from Malaysia, a family got into an accident.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The parents passed away from the accident, leaving behind two young children.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In June 2014, a five-year-old boy had to spend more than 100 days in hospital and was permanently paralysed on the right side of his body after a delivery driver failed to keep a proper lookout or a safe distance on the expressway.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me, Sir, before I move on to other aspects of the Bill, to also speak up on behalf of drivers and pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Personal mobility devices (PMDs) travelling fast and recklessly, sometimes dart out onto the road from pavements.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a startling appearance on road crossings causes immense danger to the drivers of vehicles and other road users and can cause death or serious injury.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Pedestrians, too, suffer at the hands of reckless PMD users.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, while the focus of this Bill, which I support, is to make driving safer, I hope the authorities and the Courts can consider the serious role of reckless PMD users in causing accidents on our roads and on our pedestrian or road crossings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That should reduce the culpability of the driver of the vehicle.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The other concern I have, before going in particular into the details of this Bill, is about turning into a road where the traffic light is green, while at the same time a green man allows a pedestrian to cross the same road.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The presence of a green light and a simultaneous green man can cause confusion and accidents can happen.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To avoid such confusion, would the rules allow for a green arrow to be coupled with a red man, or a green man to be coupled with a red arrow?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will make the road safer for drivers and pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If needed, this is possible and the traffic flow allows for such permutations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such offences include certain instances of dangerous driving, driving without due care and drink-driving.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are also longer suspension periods under clause 8.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, the new section 46(2)(b) also allows a licence to be suspended after the person completes a prescribed course on safe driving.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This prevents further road traffic offences not just by taking the driver off the road for a certain amount of time but also by correcting certain driving practices.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In relation to disqualification periods, is there supposed to be a difference between how the new section 65(6) and the new section 64(2D) operate?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The words of both proposed sections are the same but the relevant paragraphs in the explanatory statements are different.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second paragraph on clause 13 in the Explanatory Statement states that the disqualification periods "serve as a guide to the Court as the Court retains discretion whether to order the disqualification or depart from what is in the section." On the other hand, the second paragraph on clause 14 says that "Under the amended section 65, a Court that convicted a person of an offence under subsection (1) must in certain cases order that the person be disqualified from holding or obtaining a driving licence for a period starting on the date of the person's conviction, or the date of the person's release from prison." Would the Minister or the Senior Parliamentary Secretary kindly clarify how these proposed sections would operate?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Disqualifications do not just prevent future traffic offences, they also deter potential traffic offences from happening.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This second theme of the Bill can also be seen in enhanced punishments and the forfeiture of vehicles.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One of the crimes that has enhanced punishment is section 67 driving under the influence of drugs or alcohol.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Under clause 17, the punishment for drink-driving is roughly doubled.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The new section 65AA under clause 15 also provides for forfeiture of the vehicle in certain circumstances, such as where the driver was drink-driving and whose reckless driving or driving without due care caused death or grievous hurt.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides ensuring that there is sufficient deterrence against drink-driving, we should also ensure that the victim of a drink-driving accident can obtain compensation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When I asked the Minister for Transport in October last year during a Parliamentary Question, the reply was "Insurance policies cannot be restricted from paying out for such liabilities incurred from drink-driving." However, at least some motor insurance policies have exemption clauses that say that the insurance company "shall not be liable in respect of: 1.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Any accident, loss, damage or liability caused sustained or incurred:…(b) whilst any Insured Vehicle in respect of which indemnity is provided by this Policy is: …(iii) being driven by the Policyholder or by any person on the order of or with the permission of the Policyholder whilst under the influence of intoxicating liquor or drugs." The victim in drink-driving accidents is put in a hard position as the drink-driver may not have enough money on hand to pay the victim.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would be exacerbated if the drink-driver’s vehicle is forfeited under clause 15 of this Bill as the drink-driver would be less able to secure a loan.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am not saying that you should not forfeit the vehicle.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am in favour of forfeiting the vehicle.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My concern is for the victim of a drink-driving accident being compensated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, does the Ministry have any plans to ensure that there is support for victims of drink-driving accidents, whether it be ensuring that there be financial compensation or whether it be counselling to overcome any trauma from the incident?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides controlling the situation through the introduction of deterrent, preventive and calibrated punishment regimes, what is the demographic of the drivers for the bulk of accidents and apprehensions made due to traffic offences?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: According to the General Insurance Association's review in 2018, the 4% dip in accident reports was largely attributable to fewer private-hire cars and taxis on the road.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How are road safety education and campaign efforts effectively targeting these more "at-risk" demographics?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What are the common root reasons for accidents?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When there is change in traffic lights or roads, what is being done to lower the risk of accidents happening?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, what plans does the Ministry have to enhance road safety to keep up with changing challenges, such as a possible increase in delivery motorbicycles, cyclists and even users of e-scooters or other PMDs who choose to flout the rules against riding on the roads?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another group of offences with enhanced penalties I would like to draw attention to is that of driving without a licence, or employing or permitting another to drive without a licence, under suspension, or under disqualification.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, in the case of driving without a licence or permitting or employing someone to drive without a licence, the current section 43 of the Road Traffic Act does not specify a penalty.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is the rationale for raising the penalties?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will the proposed enhanced punishment be overly harsh on individuals who may have unknowingly driven a vehicle without a licence, for example, those above the age of 65 who were unaware that their licence had expired, or whatever the age cap for that is?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The third theme of the Bill I want to speak on is calibration.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill better calibrates the punishment meted out for the particular circumstance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is most evident by the punishment regime in clauses 13 and 14 relating to dangerous driving and driving without due care in sections 64 and 65.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Why is unauthorised speed trials and competition pegged to driving without due care or reasonable consideration under the new section 65(5)(a) and (b) and not reckless or dangerous driving under the new section 64(2C)(a) and (b)?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Unauthorised competitions are deliberate and extremely dangerous, sometimes clocking speeds that more than triple the prescribed speed limit.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although clause 15 provides that a vehicle may be forfeited for certain driving dangerously or without due care, they focus on drink-driving and are ill-suited to address illegal racing as racers may not be drunk when driving.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is it the case that the prosecution has to choose between possible forfeiture of the car and a higher possible sentence of reckless driving when charging for a situation involving illegal racing?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would give the Court a clearer picture of the driver's driving practices and habits so that the various principles of sentencing can be more accurately weighed out.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In closing, Sir, I hope that educative aspects of prevention will also supplement these changes in the law to enhance the consequences of certain offences for deterrence and prevention.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the whole, this Bill prevents and deters road traffic offences and provides for a better calibrated punishment system and, therefore, I support it.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Last month, I was knocked down by a bus, a big, lumbering double-decker to be exact.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: On the evening of 13 June, at about 8.15 pm, I was crossing the road at the junction of Upper Changi Road East and Somapah Road on my way to the Singapore University of Technology and Design to meet my students.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: They had developed a game to educate the public about fake news and were excited to demonstrate it to me.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: And by the way, the game is brilliant.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Coming back to me at the road junction, I had waited for the light to turn green in my favour and proceeded to walk once it did so.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I assure the Members of the House that at no point was I using my phone and that I was single-mindedly focused on making my way across as briskly as possible.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: When I was about three quarters of the way to the other side, I suddenly felt something very large looming over me and I turned to my left to see a double-decker about this close to me.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I was stunned and I even made eye contact with the driver and caught his horrified expression as he saw me.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The next thing I knew, I had been thrown onto my back and I felt my head hitting the road very, very hard.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: At that point, I literally saw stars, those in my head and those in our beautiful night sky although I could not quite tell which was which.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Thankfully, I did not lose consciousness and managed to scramble to the side of the road while the bus driver pulled over.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: He alighted to inquire as to my well-being and we exchanged information.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In spite of my shocked and injured state, I felt profound sympathy for the bus captain.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: He looked highly stressed, likely worried about the consequences of the accident.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As an occasional driver myself, I certainly do not wish to be in that position.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Luckily for the both of us, I walked away from the accident largely unscathed.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I endured severe aching for the next few days but fortunately did not suffer from any fractures or concussions.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, I am truly grateful that I can stand here today to deliver this speech.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: My accident gave me much to think about, but especially in relation to road safety.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: What could have caused the bus captain to completely overlook my presence on a well-lit road when traffic was light, I clearly had right of way, and also had ample time to cross the junction.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Was it a case of a driver whose shift was too long or who had had insufficient days of rest?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Or was it an issue of the discretionary right turns, leading drivers to make a quick turn when there is no on-coming traffic, but forgetting that pedestrians, too, have the right of way?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: What exactly are the safeguards we have in place to prevent an accident like mine from recurring?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, my friends remarked that had I been a child or a senior citizen, that the impact of the accident would have been that much more severe.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I, therefore, reached out to the bus company to understand more about their safety procedures.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Two members of its senior management met with me and addressed all my queries.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Such information helps the company determine how reckless or safety-conscious their drivers are.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Using such data, bus captains are effectively graded for their driving performance and the information is conveyed to them via a mobile app so that they can regulate and modulate their own driving as necessary.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Following the suspension, he underwent a day of retraining where his driving was assessed by a supervisor, before he was deemed roadworthy and returned to service.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Incidentally, the telematics data revealed that he was consistently one of their safest drivers, which perhaps helps to explain why I am still here today!

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As a regular public transport commuter, I am reassured that this much attention is paid to safety.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, it is encouraging that we have harnessed technology to better guide our bus captains, helping them to maintain good safety habits and driving standards.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: And yet, accidents do and will happen, and we should strive to further reduce their number.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, when I mentioned my accident to friends and acquaintances, they immediately raised the problem of discretionary right-turn junctions without my prompting.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Colleagues and students who also use the junction where my accident occurred mentioned witnessing many near misses between cars and pedestrians, and cars and PMD riders.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Drivers wait anxiously in the right-turn box and make a dash for it when they note the absence of oncoming traffic, overlooking the fact that there could also be pedestrians crossing at the same time.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I am not aware of the latest figures since that period, but my accident surely was not the only one.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Clearly, such junctions that allow cars and people to cross simultaneously present distinct hazards.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: They require alertness and concentration on the part of everyone.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: But when we factor in that drivers, pedestrians and PMD riders may be increasingly distracted by their mobile devices, we have a veritable formula for disaster.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: My accident left me with several important takeaways.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The first is that we have a public transport system that prioritises and invests in safety, of which we can be justifiably proud.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The second is that we should consider whether public buses can be equipped with superior sensors to better alert drivers to the presence of pedestrians and other vehicles so as to avoid collisions as far as possible.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The third takeaway is that in our Smart Nation efforts, urban analytics can be strategically marshalled to more accurately track vehicular and human traffic at all junctions, so that we can optimise traffic light timings to allow drivers and pedestrians to share the road efficiently, but also safely.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: With such analytics, we can better design junctions to allow for smooth flowing traffic, without increased cost to human lives.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: A well-functioning transport network is critical not just to our economy but also to the well-being of our citizens, ensuring that people and places are connected seamlessly but also safely.

text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay)  : I have read the news report on a survey conducted by the Traffic Police recently that involved 1,000 road users.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The results of this survey revealed that most car users thought positively of themselves when asked to rate their level of safety and graciousness on the roads.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, they felt that the level of safety and graciousness of other drivers were not that good.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is quite worrying because it reflects the mentality and attitude of drivers in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If all drivers only think of themselves, this will result in more hazards and accidents on the roads.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is important for us to continue encouraging positive behaviour on the roads.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In addition, I have also read a report about the increase in feedback on irresponsible drivers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Although the number of accidents may have gone down in general, every accident is one too many.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Serious accidents can cause injuries and death and we must do our best to avoid them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One way is by strengthening legislation to stop bad behaviour on the roads.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I hope that apart from legislation, we can also double our efforts to enhance awareness and educate the public about the importance of safety and graciousness on the roads.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I read with interest the news report on the outcome of the survey conducted by the Traffic Police recently.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The nationwide study which involved 1,000 respondents from various groups, including car drivers, taxi drivers and the elderly, revealed that most car users thought positively of themselves when asked to rate their level of safety and graciousness.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, when it came to rating the behaviour of others, most thought negatively of other drivers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I find this both slightly amusing and worrying.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I drive and when I am on the road, there would be instances when I felt that the drivers are so inconsiderate, especially when they do not give way to me.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, I am sure, there may be moments when others would have thought the same of me, too.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On a more serious and at a deeper level though, this finding reflects the mentality of Singaporean drivers and I feel that it is important to continue to nudge behaviours and develop a culture of safe and gracious driving.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also note an earlier news report sharing that the penalties for irresponsible driving in Singapore is less severe than in some other jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Further, it was mentioned that although the number of traffic accidents has dropped, the feedback on irresponsible driving has gone up.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The annual statistics from the Traffic Police showed that while there were fewer traffic accidents last year, the number of drink-driving accidents and motorists who ran red lights went up.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Motorcyclists who were drink-driving and got involved in accidents increased by 51.3% to 59 cases in 2018, from 39 cases in 2017.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, the number of people arrested for drink-driving decreased despite an increase in the number of drink-driving enforcement operations conducted in 2018.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is 7,311 cases more than 2017's 46,599 violations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Accidents caused by red light running increased slightly by 2.6% to 120 accidents, from 117 accidents in 2017.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Statistics aside, traffic accidents can have severe consequences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the more serious accidents, lives are lost and one life lost is one too many.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is, therefore, important to continue to encourage safe driving and shape the behaviours of road users.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Our traffic laws and rules are, indeed, one way to shape behaviours on the road and it may be time to further strengthen the penalties to target the egregious offences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I welcome the enhancements introduced in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would like, however, to make some comments on the amendments.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The proposed amendment also sets out a framework for the submission of any representations or objections.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note from the proposed sections 35B (2) and (3) that the DCP could proceed to revoke the licence on the proposed revocation date if the appeal is rejected.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I ask because there may be some people who depend on driving for their livelihood.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They may still remain hopeful after submitting representations and may need further time before the final implementation for the revocation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that there needs to be a balance between the need to quickly take errant drivers off the roads and to ensure fairness in the process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would just like to seek clarification on whether the DCP has the discretion to extend the notice period before revocation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My second point also relates to those who drive for a living.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I suspect that because of the length of time they spend on the roads, because they may be subjected to the vagaries of passenger demands and road conditions or because they may have become over-confident as they are quite familiar with driving, they may statistically be more likely to commit more traffic offences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I wonder if we have done any analysis on the circumstances of the traffic offenders so that there could be a more targeted approach to address the issue.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Because I believe that aside from creating deterrence and penalties, we really should look into shaping the behaviour of drivers and understanding perhaps some of the challenges drivers face and address them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My third point is a general point related to the above.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As noted earlier, alongside the enhancements of penalties, I believe there is a necessity to strengthen awareness and encourage safe driving.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think perhaps we could look at generating strong awareness of driving etiquette in specific situations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am sure a lot of things are taught before one gets a licence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, the lived experience on the roads may be different.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, I hope that all parties and agencies will continue in the effort to create awareness and build better habits and culture on the roads in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I feel emphasis should also be placed on three other areas.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One, educating road users; two, improving road engineering; and three, having safer features in vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As mentioned by the hon Member before me, Ms Rahayu Mahzam, we should do more to push out the message on the importance of being responsible road users.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To this end, I hope the regulators can strengthen the role played by and properly resource the Singapore Road Safety Council.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will allow it to mount publicity programmes to educate the public and road users and do so sustainably.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the weekend, I attended a road safety event by the Council in the Orchard Road area.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That is a good initiative and more can be done, perhaps more so in the neighbourhoods and in schools.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps also consider participating in the National Day post-parade event whereby we can get all the different road users to do a safety march with regard to sending the message about road safety.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But going upstream then, what can we do?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should review the current driving course content to ensure new learners and drivers who are taking refresher courses appreciate the need for safer driving habits.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I read that, in some cities, it was even reported that serious road offenders are made to visit the hospital morgue to realise the severity of their actions.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can probably drive home the same point on the importance of safe driving through either video replays or re-enactments in our training courses on how careless driving can result in serious accidents.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Commuters travelling in a taxi or private hire car can also do their part.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recently had an accident whereby a private hire driver collided into the rear end of my vehicle.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He mentioned that he was distracted by his passenger who suddenly, at the last minute, asked him to change direction.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As he was listening to the passenger, he did not pay attention to the road and the vehicle in front of him.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On engineering, the design of roads can also affect the safety of road users.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: LTA conducts regular reviews, for which we are grateful for, to ensure our roads are safe for motorists and pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have seen examples, such as Silver Zones for the elderly and School Zone programmes for school students.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should continue to identify and add such features in more of our estates.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More recently, LTA has started to roll out more Red Amber Green (RAG) arrows at major traffic junctions.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Recently, we recalled an accident at Clementi Road whereby one of the undergraduates had a tragic accident.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Motorists have to wait for the arrow to turn green before making a right turn.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad to know that LTA has been conscientiously installing road safety features, including turning pockets, lighted road studs and "Give Way to Pedestrian" signs, to ensure safety and smooth traffic flow.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, accidents that do not involve injuries are sometimes not reported to the Traffic Police.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I wonder how such data of vulnerable roads or roads with more accidents are being collated to understand whether or not such interventions, such as road designs or re-engineering, can slow down vehicles and minimise accident rates.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That entails having more safety features in our vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some new vehicles today are fitted with safety devices, such as auto-brake functions that automatically slow down the vehicle if they sense a pedestrian or car in the path of travel; or adaptive cruise control which automatically adjusts the vehicle speed to maintain a safe distance from vehicles ahead.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some owners install radar sensors or cameras to help them gauge and monitor the safety distance between vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Others rely on reverse sensors which alert the driver when the car is about to hit an object.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such devices serve as safety features that help drivers to navigate in a safer manner.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should also leverage telematics to reinforce good driving habits.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recently spoke to the third-party private hire app called Grab.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They send day-to-day weekly driving reports to their drivers to nudge them towards safer driving.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, we have such a scheme called the early turnover whereby we encourage early replacement of polluting vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Surely, safety vehicles should be the next in line.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond the law, I believe we can channel our efforts to cultivate responsible road users and for everybody to have a safer commute.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Cost considerations can be overcome if appropriate rebates and nudges can be put in place to speed up the adoption of safer vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I found a recent example whereby an insurance company has offered lower premiums to motorists if they respond accurately to a series of questions on safer driving.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That is a wonderful nudge for many who may not be able to be prompted to understand the importance of safer driving.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is one of the safest countries for road travel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We do have some gaps, such as our policies allowing carriage of passengers in the cargo space in goods vehicles, and our new vehicle standards, which do not require the latest electronic safety advances, such as electronic stability control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these advances are mandated in the United States (US) and European Union (EU).

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But overall, we compare well in road safety even when compared to highly developed countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A key part of maintaining road traffic safety is how we manage routine traffic offences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The vast majority of these offences will have been dealt with by composition offer or fine penalty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Fines are an important part of our road traffic safety system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This was the first review in nearly 20 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Unsurprisingly, because incomes have gone up since then, fines were raised across the board, with the steepest increases for the most severe offences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: First, can we design an optimal traffic fine schedule, based on evidence and economic principles?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Second, can we improve equity and efficiency by implementing fines that step up, linked to the income or wealth of the offender?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The economic principle for fine setting, as laid out in 1974 by the Nobel Prize winning economist Gary Becker, is that the expected fine, the penalty adjusted by the probability of being caught, should equal the social costs caused by the offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The reason is that many crimes are actions which have private benefits, but which produce external social costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We speed because we enjoy a private benefit from getting to the destination faster, or because we enjoy driving faster.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But because we are speeding, we impose an external social cost on others from the increased accident risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is also the risk of injury to the speeding driver, but that is a private cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The optimal fine makes the potential speeder realise that if they speed, they must pay the external social costs of doing so, which then deters them from speeding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Applying this principle of aligning fines to the marginal social costs is quite difficult in practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We know that speeding is dangerous, but I do not think any country has attempted to seriously quantify the cost of speeding and link these costs to fines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: One complication is that the relationship between speed and the risk of injury and death is non-linear and it increases sharply with speed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the report I referenced earlier, the WHO states that, in principle, a 1% increase in mean speed produces a 4% increase in the fatal crash risk, and a 3% increase in a serious crash risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This means that optimal fines should increase significantly as the rate of excess speed increases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Do we reflect this principle in our fine schedule for speeding?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Exceeding the road speed limit by 31 kilometres per hour (km/h) to 40 km/h carries double the fine and demerit points at $300 and eight demerit points than exceeding the speed limit by one km/h to 20 km/h does, at $150 and four demerit points.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: An evidence-based optimal fine setting policy would examine whether the harm caused by speeding 31 km/h to 40 km/h above the limit is, in fact, larger than double that of speeding only one km/h to 20 km/h.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The fines and demerit points should be revised upwards according to the actual risks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It would be useful if the Ministry could publish the results of any studies conducted that would show the evidence basis for our recent revisions to the fine schedule.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A second issue with setting optimal fines is that motorists differ greatly in their income and wealth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, fines are generally equal when different motorists commit the same offence, which creates a problem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A fine that is large enough to be meaningful and appropriate to punish the average motorist may be too large for lower-income motorists and too small for the richest motorists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is an obvious limitation to optimal fines in practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Fines do not work if they are so large that people cannot pay and fines also do not work if they are not meaningful deterrents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Elected Members know that many appeals at Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS) are for traffic and parking offences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In most cases, the resident admits to committing the offence, but they appeal for leniency because the fines will cause them financial hardship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This creates a challenge when we want to increase fines to appropriately deter unsafe driving.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While all motorists should drive safely, we must be mindful that a significant penalty for the average private car driver is actually an immense sum for the vocational driver.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is evidence that fines do deter unsafe driving and that fines have price effects, that is, higher fines are more effective at deterring unsafe driving, as long as the driver feels the pinch from paying the fine.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In a study by Bar-Ilan and Sacerdote published in the Journal of Law and Economics in 2004, the authors studied what happened after Israel raised the fine for red-light violations by 150% in 1996.
