speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The authors had demographic data of drivers, which allowed them to understand which groups of motorists changed behaviour more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But what is interesting is who was affected more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I interpret these results as supportive of the theory that fines do deter unsafe driving, and moreover, the deterrent effect of fines depends on the income or wealth of the offender.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Richer offenders simply feel the pinch of a fine less.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: One way of ensuring that fines have the appropriate deterrent effect, while keeping the financial impact on vocational drivers in mind, is to calibrate fines based on the income or wealth of the offending motorist.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Not all speeders in Finland pay so much.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A more typical motorist would have paid only €345 for the same offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The reason why the unfortunate businessman paid so much is that he was one of Finland's highest income earners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Speeding is an offence which is punishable by day-fines in Finland.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A similar day-fine system is in use in a number of countries, mostly Scandinavian.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The legal history is that a fine represents a payment in lieu of jail, and being locked up is more costly for a high-income offender, because the lost income is larger.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, the fine paid "per day" of jail should be scaled to income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Finnish businessman's speeding offence was rated at eight days' worth of fines and, given his high income, this worked out to €54,024.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In case anyone is thinking I am suggesting we charge S$50,000 speeding fines, let me state for the record that I think this is probably too high, even for our "fine city".

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we could revise our traffic fine penalty system to ensure that fines appropriately deter high-income motorists, while being fair and reasonable for lower-income motorists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These form most vehicles on the road, and differences in the income of drivers of private cars can be very large in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think it is reasonable to presume that the driver of a large luxury car is able to pay more than one driving a cheaper vehicle, and they would likely regard the demerit points and other consequences of an offence as far more serious than the fine itself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, insofar as many luxury cars are marketed as safer than less well-equipped cars, there is even more reason to increase the optimal fine as a deterrent, since the perceived risk of injury to the driver themselves will be lower and luxury car drivers may be more inclined to speed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But there is room for improvement in how we design our fine penalty system, which is a major component of road safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should examine the evidence basis behind the social cost of unsafe driving and design fines, particularly for higher speeds, to reflect the actual risks more appropriately.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We can also improve equity and efficiency by calibrating fines according to the income or wealth of the offending motorist.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As road traffic safety is an evolving problem, I hope the Government will study these issues when planning the next revision of the RTA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I stand in support of the general rationale behind the amendments but would like to seek clarifications on two areas relating to the obligations of drivers in accidents involving animals and the legal effect of compounded offences under the RTA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The campaign started before I was elected as a Member of Parliament and continued when I became a Member.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have raised this issue in this House in 2016 and the then Senior Minister of State Desmond Lee replied that the definition of "animals" in the RTA will be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am delighted that we are now proposing amendments to this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The current definition no longer makes sense. "Animal" means any horse, cattle, ass, mule, sheep, pig, goat or dog.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under the RTA, motorists are required to stop and help these animals if they are knocked down.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that "The original intent of that legislation was to ensure restitution to their owners should an accident occur".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the days of having horses, cattles, asses, mules, sheep, pigs and goats on our roads are long gone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, our legislation needs to be updated to keep up with the times.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The unfortunate reality is that we now have other animals on our roads, a lot of them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a long list of animals, including cats, civets, pangolins, wild boars, monkeys and snakes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The other unfortunate reality is that these animals are often knocked down.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At times, they are not killed, and could recover if help is provided.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As the Minister had previously stated, "The question is whether we should now mandatorily require all motorists to stop, should they hit an animal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They should stop, if it is safe to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the motorist requires assistance in relation to attending to the animal, he can contact the Agri-Food and Veterinary Authority of Singapore (AVA) or the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SPCA)." They can also call Animal Concerns Research and Education Society (ACRES).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is in line with what the animal welfare groups have called for, but I have some concerns about this amendment and would like to seek some clarification.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The effect of the current amendment is that a driver who runs into any animal may have an obligation to stop, regardless of the species of the animal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An animal could be anything from a dog to a lizard.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Taken to the extreme, this provision could have ridiculous implications.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I agreed that we need to expand the definition of "animal" beyond the current definition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I also appreciate the difficulty of coming up with a definition to limit the scope of this provision.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, removing the definition altogether seems to be a blunt measure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It simply shifts the burden of making this difficult judgement to the driver.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are asking a driver, driving a fast-moving vehicle, to make an instantaneous judgement on whether the animal is likely to have an owner, or whether the injured or dead animal would pose a safety hazard to other road users.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is it really safer to require a driver to divert attention away from the road to make this judgement call?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would there be a loophole in that a driver can just say that it was not safe to stop, so he or she did not stop?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To provide some guidance for drivers, can the Minister or the Senior Parliamentary Secretary provide more clarification on how a driver can determine if an animal is likely to pose a safety hazard and how it intends to enforce this provision?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will the Traffic Police determine if it was safe for a driver to stop and render assistance?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would it be better to amend the definition of "animal" to include more animals rather than remove the definition altogether?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In that case, the Court decided that it may take into account compounded offences under the RTA for the purpose of sentencing as they form part of the offender's bad driving record.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 139AA affirms and gives statutory force to this High Court decision.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may raise some concerns because of the prevailing legal principle that compounding an offence amounts to an acquittal in law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is expressly stated in sections 241 and 242 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) for Penal Code offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This rule equally applies to non-Penal Code offences as held in the High Court decision of Rajamanikam Ramachandran vs Chan Teck Yuen.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Allowing a compounded offence to be taken into consideration for sentencing removes another distinction between an acquittal and a conviction that may be perceived as an erosion of the presumption of innocence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister K Shanmugam said in an oral answer to a Parliamentary Question in August 2008, “the presumption of innocence is an important and fundamental principle and is one of the foundations of our Criminal Justice System.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They may do so believing that there would be no adverse impact if composition amounts to acquittal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Their decision may change if they are now told that the compounded offence remains on the record and may affect sentencing for future offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to thank MHA for responding positively to the concerns raised by the animal welfare groups.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the aim behind the Bill which is to deter irresponsible driving that may lead to harming of innocent lives and damage to property.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I applaud the Ministry for obtaining feedback from the public before presenting this Bill for consideration in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In particular, in this Bill, I support the calibration of punishment depending on the harm caused by the motorist in driving his vehicle dangerously or carelessly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Indeed, I note that the Supreme Court, in several recent decisions dealing with sentencing of motorists who are convicted for offences, such as drink-driving, dangerous driving and careless driving, already apply an analytical framework which requires a consideration of the harm caused by the motorist as well as his culpability.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have a query on the proposal to provide for enhanced punishment for a "serious offender" who commits the offence of dangerous driving or careless driving. "Serious Offender" is defined in the amendment Bill as a person convicted for drink-driving or, alternatively convicted for refusing to give his breath sample.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because, as mentioned before, in the current sentencing framework, the harm and culpability of a drink-driver would be taken into consideration in relation to a sentence imposed on a drink-driver under section 67.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But we cannot have one analytical framework for sentencing in relation to drink-driving if a person is charged singly, as opposed to another situation if he is charged for drink-driving as well as dangerous driving.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, I would welcome a clarification from the hon Minister as to what is the Ministry's expectation in relation to sentencing under the proposed sections 64 and 65.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The next query I have is in relation to the applicability of community sentencing options.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have previously spoken about the desirability to widen sentencing options during an Adjournment Motion in this House on 11 September 2017.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I pointed out that then, for drink-driving cases, the person on conviction would not be liable for community sentencing but a motorist who was convicted for causing death by a negligent act under the Penal Code was imposed a community sentence of a short detention order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was because the sentence for drink-driving offence under the RTA was fixed in law with a minimum mandatory sentence of a fine.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my respectful view, for traffic cases involving people behaving negligently or not realising that they exceeded the alcohol limit but who have caused low to medium levels of harm to life and property, community sentences may be a good option for them in terms of addressing the sentencing principles of deterrence as well as just deserts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Subsequently, in March 2018, this House passed amendments to the CPC to expand the list of offences for which community sentences may be imposed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the amended section 337(3) of the CPC, a Court may impose a community work order even if the offender is convicted of an offence for which a mandatory minimum sentence of a fine is prescribed by law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would welcome the hon Minister’s confirmation that this comports with the policy intent behind this amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I may be wrong, but one community sentencing option which does not appear to be open for offenders under the RTA in relation to offences under the proposed sections 64 and 65 is the short detention order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If a person is imposed with a short detention order, unlike an imprisonment, his conviction would not constitute as a registrable crime under the Registration of Criminals Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would have thought that, particularly for lower-level culpability acts leading to medium-level harm, a short detention order should be considered as a suitable punishment so that the accused would not be delivered with a disproportionate crushing blow vis-a-vis his prospects in the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder why this option is not provided for in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The next point I wish to make relates to the fact that the sentencing provision in section 69 of the RTA, which deals with administration of preliminary breath tests, is being retained in its current form even though the sentencing provisions for section 67 are proposed to be enhanced.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In both situations, a first-timer would be liable on conviction to a fine of not less than $1,000 and not more than $5,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A repeat offender would similarly be liable for a fine of not less than $3,000 and not more than $10,000 and to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do appreciate that if a person does not provide a breath sample for a preliminary breath test, he may be arrested nonetheless and be required to submit a breath sample for the prescribed breathalyser test at the Police station.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, given that there is currently an existing parity between the sentences provided for both provisions and the aim of this Bill is to deter motorists from irresponsible behaviour, I wonder what is the policy reason for not similarly proposing to amend the punishment for section 69(4) of the RTA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also would like to ask if we have sufficiently leveraged advances made in technology.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The prescribed breathalyser test was introduced in 1996.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It was contemplated then that the test has to be administered in the Police station.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also a potential for removing the need to administer preliminary breath test.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They will also be required to blow on a second occasion at a random time to limit the chances of others blowing into the breathalyser for them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for an update from the hon Minister on this front.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The final point I wish to make relates to making owners and operators of vehicles who cause death or injuries as a result of mechanical failure arising from negligent maintenance of their vehicles, especially heavy vehicles.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have spoken on this topic in this House recently.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I appreciate that these amendments are being introduced by the Minister for Home Affairs and the focus is, therefore, on driver conduct.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would respectfully suggest that MOT take a look at the RTA with a view to tighten the framework so that such owners are held responsible for death and injuries arising from their neglect.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also suggest that the Ministry consider making some safety measures mandatory to protect other road users and this is a call that was made by the hon Member Mr Ang Hin Kee as well as the hon Member Assoc Prof Walter Theseira.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are also discussions in several countries about making the installation of dash cams compulsory, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Dash cams can be a deterrent against irresponsible driving, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister mentioned about video footage being referred to the Police for investigation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are also a good source of evidence for investigation into RTA offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some dash cams have anti-collision sensors and could have made a difference, for example, in relation to the accident that the hon Nominated Member of Parliament Prof Lim Sun Sun was involved in.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am so glad that she is none the worse for it.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If the victim is injured, it means that he has to take time off work, which could result in loss of income or employment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In more serious cases when the victim sustains a disability, or even death, entire lives and families are damaged irreversibly.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I had a bubbly young resident in her mid-30s.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She was a restaurant manager in the country club in the Jurong area.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On her way home to Yishun, at the traffic junction of Lentor Avenue and Yio Chu Kang Road, when the traffic light turned green in her favour, she went straight towards Khatib but a car turned right hastily and knocked her down.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Her mother fell ill soon after that and passed away.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is how a reckless driver ruined a family.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Meanwhile, perpetrators might get off with a fine.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, such people are a menace on the roads and should have their licence revoked immediately.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Very often, my residents told me that their sleep was interrupted by the noise from the racing vehicles along Yishun Avenue 1, Yishun Street 51 and Yishun Ring Road.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This happens, especially on Friday night and Saturday night.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They need not sleep, but my residents need to sleep.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Besides the obvious examples of dangerous driving, there have been previous grievous accidents which occurred because the driver did not have sufficient rest or was driving while on medication that would impair driving ability or if the vehicle was not maintained in good condition.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In a recent high-profile accident, a veteran rugby coach was fatally hit by a runaway tyre while riding a motorcycle.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Would such cases be classified as dangerous driving?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I note that there are no specific regulations or benchmarks when it comes to determining such conditions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, we need to have a public conversation about dangerous and careless driving.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even as we move towards a car-lite society, it is concerning that there are more incidents of dangerous and careless driving.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What are the reasons for this increase in road accidents?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Given that the top cause of accidents in Singapore is failing to keep a proper lookout or distracted driving, how can we better enforce the ban on using smartphones while driving?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A survey last year revealed that nearly one in two Singapore drivers feel that the roads have become less safe than they were three years ago and the reasons for these include more aggressive drivers, more non-motorists on the roads, including cyclists and PMDs, and more private hire vehicles.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is it time to examine the need to strike a healthier balance among the types of users on the roads?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should also look into addressing the increase in aggressive driving, whether it is due to frustration at the road conditions or due to stress and other personal reasons.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Although PMDs, aside from bicycles and e-bikes, are not explicitly covered under this Bill, I would like to remind the Ministry that some PMDs do go onto the roads, whether legally or not.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The survey I cited just now showed that drivers feel unsafe because of them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many drivers have seen them zig-zagging in many parts of Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How many such drivers have been caught by the Traffic Police?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Countries like Germany and Peru have banned PMDs on footpaths, and France has just announced that they will ban PMDs on footpaths from September.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many cities have built dedicated cycling and PMD lanes on the roads.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: That would help both drivers and pedestrians feel safer.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How can a three-year-old kid be hit by an e-scooter in a shopping mall?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How can our commuters feel so unsafe while waiting for public transport at bus stops?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Also, motorised PMDs should be licensed and have their licence revoked if they hurt someone, just like in this act of zig-zagging on the road or at the bus stop.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Active Mobility Act will take some lessons from the Road Safety Act and implement stricter deterrent measures.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to talk about jaywalkers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A resident shared with me that he was involved in a road accident because of a jaywalker.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If I may use his language, he said:  (In Mandarin)  : "(The jaywalker) didn't cross the road earlier or later; he happened to cross the road right in front of my car!" So, an accident happened.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: According to what my resident had told me, the Traffic Police only warned the jaywalker, but my resident was prosecuted in Court.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This amendment will allow us to deal with reckless driving more quickly and severely.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government can also explore the following areas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The first is relating to driving without sufficient sleep, under drug influence or when the vehicle condition is bad.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If we can specify the rules and clearly forbid these behaviours, a deterrent effect can be achieved.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: According to surveys, motorists have expressed that PMDs on roads make them feel unsafe.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, we should check more frequently whether there are PMDs riding on roads illegally.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When we build new towns, we should have designated bicycle and PMD lanes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If there is an accident, the licence can be revoked.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, there are more and more traffic offences.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, the heavier penalties, including longer imprisonment and disqualification from driving, should have a stronger deterrent effect.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, it would be better if we could put in place preventive measures to minimise the possibility of drivers committing offences in the first place.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One problem, which has persistently bothered me and many of my present and former Parliamentary colleagues, is the hazardous practice of having Green Man and lights for both pedestrians and turning vehicles at junctions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These signals should be consistent to reduce confusion among motorists who now encounter different signalling at different junctions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also appeal to LTA to expedite the installation of RAG.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Greater consultation with the Traffic Police, who understand how the increasing population of elderly pedestrians behave on roads, would be most helpful.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their input would inform planners, for example, on placement of pedestrian crossings, and where to build overhead bridges with ramps or elevators, since the elderly would have difficulty with steps.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin)  : The Traffic Police had noted in their 2018 Traffic Accident Situation news release that accidents involving elderly pedestrians who jaywalk remain a concern, as 25% of all accidents involving pedestrians involve elderly pedestrians.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Greater consultation with the Traffic Police, who understand how the increasing population of elderly pedestrians behave on roads, would be helpful.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their input would inform planners, for example, on placement of pedestrian crossings, and where to build overhead bridges with ramps or elevators, since the elderly would have difficulty with steps.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Finally, I would like to raise my concerns over speeding heavy vehicles.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have observed and received feedback from my residents that many of these vehicles are regularly driving at above our speed limits.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I seek clarifications on what is done when they are caught speeding.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is the time lag between a speeding vehicle captured on our road cameras and the update to the Traffic Police database, so that timely enforcement can take place?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Does the Ministry have statistics on such drivers and their vehicles for the past five years?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are serious traffic offences and are often a result of irresponsible driver behaviour.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The proposed amendments to the RTA are, therefore, timely as the harsher punishments would help deter irresponsible driving.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I would like to provide additional suggestions to help make commuting on our roads safer.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I support MHA's proposal to enhance criminal penalties to deter irresponsible driving, such as those who drink and drive.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We just simply do not drink and drive.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And I believe that we can do more to deter people from driving under the influence of alcohol.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would serve as both a legal deterrent as well as shape societal dynamics by making it a joint responsibility for others to stop someone from drink-driving.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Technology can also be a key enabler in preventing drink-driving.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Countries, such as Australia, the Netherlands and the US, have passed laws to mandate the installation of ignition-interlock devices in vehicles of convicted drink-driving offenders.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such drivers are required to take a breathalyser test installed into the vehicle, prior to being allowed to start their vehicles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to go beyond our usual business-as-usual practices of raising penalties and conducting enforcement operations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I propose that we look at how to improve the safety of our roads through enhancing road infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: An infrastructure enhancement that we can make is in the area of our traffic junctions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, let us simply do away with discretionary right turns.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Two high profile accidents in 2018, one along Clementi Road and another at the junction of Jalan Anak Bukit and Jalan Jurong Kechil, which saw two separate fatalities, bring to mind the dangers of discretionary right turns.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In both cases, the drivers appeared to have had an error of judgement in making the right turn.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Earlier, we have also heard similar cases by Members Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Prof Lim Sun Sun.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, while I am encouraged that there are plans to install more non-discretionary right-turn arrows, I would like for us to go one step further and convert all right-turn arrows into non-discretionary.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would certainly go a long way in making our roads a safer place.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, we should include countdown timers at all traffic junctions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is not my first time raising this and I note that LTA, in their reply, said that they had conducted a small-scale pilot at the junction of North Bridge Road and Rochor Road over a period of six months in 2003.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In that pilot, LTA found that there were no significant improvements to road safety.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But many countries have since implemented such countdown timers as they view that it improves road safety.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In 2017, a study published by the Oregon State University had also found that such countdown timers lead to safer responses from drivers as it reduces mistakes made in what is called the "dilemma zone", which is the area in which a driver is not sure whether to stop or keep going when the light turns yellow.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to revisit the conclusion of the pilot trial that LTA had conducted over 15 years ago.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe that the experiences of other countries are sound and there is potential for such countdown timers to further reduce traffic accidents, given the increase in red-light running violations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that the Traffic Police and LTA can conduct a new trial of traffic countdown timers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Perhaps, the agencies can consider Orchard Road, which is within my constituency, which has many traffic junctions – at least eight – and which has significantly heavy traffic flow, for this new trial.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to do more education to teach both cyclists and motorcyclists on the importance of defensive riding, as they are our most vulnerable group of road-users.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is not unusual to see motorcyclists riding in between lanes, especially during peak-hour traffic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some would even manoeuvre at a fast speed zig-zagging across lanes and in between vehicles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This puts them at risk of being side-swept by vehicles if they are in a blind spot.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More needs to be done to educate our motorcyclists on the dangers of riding between lanes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Correspondingly, we need to educate other drivers on the importance of checking their blind spots constantly before making a turn or making a lane change.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to make another pitch again to disallow cyclists from plying our bus lanes during operating hours.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many cyclists do not cycle in a single file and, even if some do, the bus lanes are simply not wide enough to provide a safety distance between the bus and the cyclist.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope the agencies would consider my suggestions which I believe would serve to further make our roads safer.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, protecting the rights of all road users while continuing to enhance accessibility has increasingly come into tension.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is not unique to Singapore but certainly more challenging for us, given our high-density urban environment of 7,804 people per square (sq) km.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These challenges will only exacerbate, with one in four Singaporeans to be aged 65 and above by 2030.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Including persons with disabilities, this figure reaches a third of our residential population.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As the amendments proposed in this Bill seek to adjust penalties and improve regulatory regimes to manage this tension, I take this opportunity to speak up for the elderly and disability population to engage in the conversation of road rights and how Singapore can best enjoy limited shared spaces in a way that protects all, especially vulnerable members of our population with greater accessibility needs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Penalties and regulations are important in ensuring the safety of all road users, but they must also be complemented by understanding and acceptance by the public, which will only be possible if we have these conversations that cultivate cultural acceptance.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I acknowledge that our various public agencies recognise these needs, as reflected in the latest Land Transport Master Plan (LTMP) 2040 and URA Draft Master Plan 2019.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, we can, and must, do more to build an inclusive, accessible Singapore while navigating the tension between safety and accessibility.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot have a conversation on the tension of accessibility and safety without bringing up the PMDs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: At the risk of going off-road here, pun intended, I seek your indulgence, Mr Deputy Speaker, as I offer another – but important – consideration, on behalf of our elderly and persons with disabilities regarding PMDs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: PMDs have grown in usage and already play an important role in the lives of people who depend on them for various forms of participation in society, especially by the elderly and differently-abled.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As 76-year-old retiree Madam Angie Ng shared, the most life-changing decision was getting a motorised scooter which allows her to go out marketing, visit friends and have a meal, tasks previously virtually impossible because of her osteoporosis which made it extremely painful for her to walk.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Other examples include Ms Juni Syafiqa Binte Jumat who landed a job with GrabFood with her electric wheelchair.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is clear the rapid proliferation of specific PMDs amplifies the need to develop a culture of safely sharing limited spaces among users going at different speeds.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: On 28 May, a news article noted that Housing and Development Board (HDB) void deck areas were exempted from the Active Mobility Act and Town Councils can impose their own rules.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While the Government works towards having every household within 300 metres of a Mass Rapid Transit station, the elderly and differently-abled still rely on their PMDs to enjoy the same privilege of access to public spaces and transport.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The physical and psychological benefits which PMDs bring cannot be underestimated.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: An outright ban on PMDs on footpaths or void decks may be a convenient but also a blunt solution.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A more effective and calibrated approach would be to institute a different extent of regulation for different PMD user-groups as well as, perhaps more importantly, cultivating a path-sharing and safe riding culture.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: AVs have opened up new possibilities to meet mobility needs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And to the vulnerable segments of our population, especially the elderly, AV deployment can both be a cause for celebration and a concern.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: With one in four of our population being 65 and above by 2030, many who have always enjoyed the freedom of mobility are now and will be less able to.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: AVs can cover the short distances to visit grandchildren who live close-by without having to navigate stairs, walkways without handrails, or traffic junctions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: LTA's vision for a car-lite Singapore includes low-speed self-driving pods for neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Both these initiatives can really benefit our seniors with more point-to-point, short-route services.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, AVs are moving vehicles which pose a risk to road users and pedestrians.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must, therefore, ensure that we balance the design and deployment of AVs with safety and mobility.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Whether or not AVs bring about higher accessibility for the elderly will clearly depend on whether we have designed the vehicles, network and system to their needs and challenges.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Reviewing the current use cases and testing compiled by Smart Nation SG, I have to humbly suggest that we may have to do more for our growing numbers of seniors.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, as pedestrians, the elderly are more likely to be at risk with AVs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Pedestrian safety studies emphasise the driver-pedestrian interaction and provisions of cues for decision-making.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In the absence of a driver, the elderly pedestrian can only rely on cues from the vehicles.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The elderly have slower reaction times and could require both enhanced visual and audio cues to be aware of oncoming traffic.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given our rapidly ageing population, AVs should be designed and tested with consideration to these safety needs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This could include braking reaction time, as well as exterior vehicle design and vehicle sound levels.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As passengers, the elderly can benefit from the convenience and safety provided by AVs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, familiarity with the technology, awareness of benefits and user-centric design are all critical aspects to acceptance of this technology.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These are not areas where the elderly population frequent, limiting their awareness of this technology and its benefits.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As always, it is better to "show them, not tell them".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Providing opportunities for the elderly to experience the technology is important.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While supportive of AV deployment, I cannot help but come back to the complexity around road rights.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, should a slower-moving AV providing point-to-point service be afforded preferential road rights to other motorised vehicles?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Do we carve out more space from sidewalks or from motorised roadways for new pickup points?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These are difficult but important questions for our society and policymakers to grapple with.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: How do we share space amongst competing users, humans or otherwise, in that perennial creative tension of road rights as well as ensuring the safety of pedestrians, cyclists and motorists?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Recognising the diverse needs for accessibility across all user groups, new modes of transportation should be harnessed to enable all Singaporeans to lead healthier, happier lives while protecting vulnerable road users.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As much as my heart aches for the lives affected and lost through misuse and accidents from the new devices, we must not throw the baby out with the bathwater either.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Diverse mobility options are clearly the future that we need to embrace.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But this future can only be realised if and when we rigorously test and design for the diversity of user experiences and needs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot neglect the discussion of fair allocation, safety and well-being.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The elderly and the differently-abled must be invited and included to participate in and negotiate on their rights as users of our shared spaces, roads and pathways.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Active participation at the community level will encourage grassroots and ground-up actions, including locale-specific solutions, that help to cultivate the gracious culture of space sharing that we aspire towards.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our biggest challenge will be in achieving true inclusivity in urban and transport planning as well as fostering a healthy culture of sharing our limited spaces in a way that keeps one another safe as new mobility technologies emerge.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This must, therefore, be our priority in our quest towards being a sustainable smart nation for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have conducted decades of public education and made continuous investments in road networks and technology to enhance safety of all users.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, the most important component of road safety is still the behaviour of our motorists.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, many motorists still have some way to go in terms of safety awareness and etiquette.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In recent years, the number of summonses issued for traffic offences and feedback letters sent to the Traffic Police have been increasing.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More worryingly, we are seeing a jump in the number of drink-driving accidents.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With lives and limbs at stake, heavier penalties, as proposed in this Bill, are necessary to serve as stronger deterrents to motorists who drive irresponsibly and dangerously.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Longer jail terms and disqualification periods (DQ) from driving will certainly help to keep such hazardous drivers off the roads.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My concern is that quite a number of disqualified drivers are not compliant.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a result, the effectiveness of DQ, as a deterrent and punishment, could be undermined.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, I would like to propose that the Ministry also consider restricting offenders' access to vehicles.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This can be partly achieved by prohibiting vehicle ownership for various durations, depending on the severity of their offences.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would mean that offenders might even have to transfer or sell their vehicles, resulting in potential inconveniences and, perhaps, financial losses.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They should not be allowed to transfer to anyone without a driving licence, of course.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I am not sure if these offenders would be prevented from acquiring another vehicle and I would like to seek some clarifications on this.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, anyone, such as family members and friends, who willingly or unwittingly provide access to vehicles should also be made to bear varying loads of penalties, so that they will be more vigilant in keeping these offenders out of the driver's seat.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Ministry should also provide car leasing companies with greater support and tools to ensure that they lease vehicles to only motorists with valid licences.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And I do applaud the move to make the licences virtual.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These companies should be able to perform cross-checking in real time and be provided updated data.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to request that the Ministry consider following the measures by the EU to install speed limiters in all new cars.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These devices automatically prevent drivers from exceeding the speed limit.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It might be even better if we could take it one step further and require all vehicles to be fitted or retrofitted with such devices.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These include automated emergency braking, electronic data recorders and features to be built into bigger and heavier vehicles like lorries to improve visibility of cyclists and pedestrians around them.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should consider incorporating these ideas as well.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, we should make it mandatory for motorists to install and maintain approved models of car cameras.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And these cameras can help to moderate driving behavior and detect other irresponsible motorists.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Adjustments to infrastructure and additional training will help keep our senior drivers safe on our roads.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should take heed of the experiences of other countries with significant elderly populations.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In June, the Lianhe Zaobao reported on an NHK article about the severe problems caused by elderly Japanese motorists.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The traffic accidents they are involved in have the highest death rates.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The main cause for the group aged 75 and above who are involved in fatal accidents was "inappropriate vehicle operation".

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Efforts would have to be made to persuade older drivers of the benefits of these assessments as they will enhance their own and other road users' safety.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: While Members recognised the importance of enforcement measures to deter irresponsible driving, many also highlighted the need to go beyond enforcement and take a wider approach to ensuring road safety, to make use of other levers, such as education and engagement.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I will respond to questions on our regulatory regime, as well as our general approach to road safety.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Second Minister for Home Affairs, Mrs Josephine Teo, will then address questions on criminal offences and touch on emerging road traffic issues.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: First, on our amendments to tighten the regulatory regime against irresponsible driving.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On the streamlined licence suspension and revocation process, Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked whether the DCP may have the discretion to extend the notice period before suspension and revocation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is because, in this case, the motorist is taking steps to address his errant behaviour.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Thus, where a licensee has indicated to Traffic Police that he intends to take the DIPS Retraining course and the course date is later than the date when the suspension is supposed to take effect, he will have the effective date of the suspension pushed back.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is so that the licensee may complete the course and have the suspension period reduced.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It bears remembering that for a motorist to be facing suspension and revocation, he would have committed several offences before, and he would have had opportunities previously to appeal against those offences.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We have to ensure that our processes are implemented fairly and consistently, a point that the hon Member Ms Rahayu Mahzam also mentioned in her speech.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: There were also questions on obligations for motorists in accidents involving animals.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We do not want to be too prescriptive in the law by stating when it is safe or unsafe, as it is not possible to cover all situations and accurately describe when it is safe or unsafe.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Similarly, it is not possible to be exhaustive in listing out all the types of animals that motorists should stop for in accidents involving animals.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police will take a practical approach and the Courts will decide, depending on the facts of the case.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members spoke on the progress of existing road safety measures and made new suggestions to improve road safety.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members spoke on the need to calibrate our approach to different road user groups.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Allow me to explain how we have done so.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the measures that have been taken to target "at-risk" road user groups.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Melvin Yong also pointed out the need to educate and engage with motorcyclists as an "at-risk" group.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In recent years, the Traffic Police have identified vulnerable road user groups, such as elderly pedestrians and motorcyclists, and taken an increasingly calibrated approach to working with these different road user groups.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, the Traffic Police regularly engage these groups through targeted regular road safety dialogues as well as outreach events, such as the annual Singapore Ride Safe.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Traffic Police also developed the Road Master Test Kit to help elderly road users assess their eyesight, hearing and reaction times and to share safe road use habits with them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam spoke about the need to engage and shape the behaviours of vocational drivers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And the Traffic Police work closely with agencies, such as MOM, MOT and LTA, to introduce measures for vocational drivers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, the Traffic Police work with the Workplace Safety and Health Council to remind heavy vehicle drivers and their employers regularly on the importance of adopting safe driving practices.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Traffic Police also engage taxi and private hire car drivers, their companies, as well as the National Taxi Association and the National Private Hire Vehicles Association on safe driving practices.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To remind taxi drivers to stay alert and drive safely when they approach high-risk areas, the Traffic Police worked with taxi companies to incorporate the locations of high-risk areas in the Mobile Data Terminals of taxis.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members also spoke about the need to continually update our measures.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Traffic Police and LTA have stepped up enforcement, education and engagement to improve road safety.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We conduct periodic reviews to ensure our measures are effective.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee asked to conduct periodic reviews of driving course content and to increase engagement initiatives to raise awareness among different road user groups.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is to allow them to practise safe driving habits in a controlled environment.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On engagement, we agree that this is important and MHA and the Traffic Police are working on extending our outreach to as many road users as possible.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu spoke about the need to cater to an ageing motorist population.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: He suggested to make adjustments to our regime, such as customised training and health assessments.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: At present, we already have calibrated health checks for motorists.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Second, Members recognised the need to explore new solutions and have raised new suggestions to improve road safety.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira suggested to scale road traffic fines according to income, to improve deterrence and allow equity in the administration of justice.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We note that some other jurisdictions, such as Finland, have implemented such an income-based system.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Other jurisdictions, such as the UK, have piloted trials that were, unfortunately, eventually discontinued.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Joan Pereira suggested for the Traffic Police to be involved in the earlier stages of infrastructural road planning.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Traffic Police work with HDB and LTA in the early stages of planning for new estates.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Traffic Police assess the likely traffic and pedestrian flow in the new HDB estates and provide advice on the specific locations where enforcement cameras ought to be installed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: One recent example is Bidadari New Town where the Traffic Police assessed and decided to install two red-light cameras.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Likewise, the Traffic Police provide inputs, where required, to LTA's road safety infrastructure plans.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Most recently, the Traffic Police worked with LTA to reduce the speed limits at two Silver Zones from 40 km/h to 30 km/h.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members also made various other suggestions, such as Mr Ang Hin Kee’s suggestion to issue rebates to car dealers who install safety-enabling technologies in their vehicles and provide training for vocational drivers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu, Prof Lim Sun Sun, Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Murali Pillai suggested to leverage new technologies, such as urban analytics, ignition-interlock devices and speed limiters.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Christopher de Souza suggested providing support for victims of drink-driving accidents.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun and Ms Joan Pereira also suggested to expedite the installation of Red-Amber-Green arrows at all right-turning junctions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu suggested to restrict offenders’ access to vehicles.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Melvin Yong suggested for LTA to consider the installation of countdown timers and to disallow cyclists from bus lanes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Murali Pillai suggested for MOT to tighten the framework such that owners are held responsible for death and injuries arising from their neglect to maintain their vehicles.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We agree with the Members that a wider approach to ensuring road safety is important.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun had an unfortunate accident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: She did not tell me when I met her yesterday.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are all relieved that she has recovered and joined Members to make an important contribution to this debate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Sun Xueling has addressed some of the Members' questions and suggestions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will deal with those regarding the enhanced criminal penalties and then the emerging road traffic issues.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, the definition of Dangerous and Careless Driving.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah raised two examples: accidents caused by drivers who had insufficient rest, and accidents caused when there is a mechanical failure of a vehicle, which Mr Murali Pillai also asked about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In general, driving when one is not in a condition to do so is more likely to be considered as dangerous rather than careless.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Having said that, other factors, such as the manner of driving, will also be taken into account.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Attorney-General's Chambers will consider the facts of each case when determining the appropriate offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, failure to maintain one's vehicle is already an offence under the RTA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, under the Workplace Safety and Health Act, employers have a duty to ensure the safety and health of their employees at work.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Failure to do so will also be an offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Christopher de Souza shared his concerns that the increased penalties for Driving without Licence and Permitting or Employing Another Person to Drive without Licence may be too harsh on individuals who may have unknowingly driven a vehicle without a licence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, a person may not be aware of the need to certify his fitness to drive and renew his licence when he turns 65.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police and the Public Prosecutor will look into the specifics of each case to decide the appropriate charge.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Another question Mr Christopher de Souza raised had to do with the treatment for motorists when the victim also violated traffic rules and contributed to the accident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about accidents caused by jaywalkers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Conversely, if the motorist was not driving safely, for instance, he spotted a pedestrian jaywalking but decided to speed up in a bid to drive past the pedestrian before the pedestrian can reach the lane his vehicle was on and hit the victim as a result, he will be prosecuted.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But, of course, the jaywalker may also be taken to task.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about Driving Under Influence offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He asked about the additional penalties for Dangerous and Careless Driving offences, for motorists who had done so while under the influence of alcohol or drugs and whether this would mean that a person is punished twice for the same act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The first, a motorist was driving under influence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second, a motorist was driving dangerously or carelessly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A motorist committing the first action, driving under influence, will be liable for penalties even if he was not driving dangerously or carelessly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked if the penalties for failing to provide a specimen for a preliminary breath test should be increased.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As the proposed penalties are lower than that for the offence of Driving Under Influence, he worries that this may create an incentive for a motorist not to provide the specimen.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At present, the Traffic Police subject motorists to two tests for suspected Driving Under Influence offences: first, a preliminary breath test to check if the breath alcohol content is beyond the legal limit; and, second, a test to measure the exact alcohol content of the motorist.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A motorist who refuses to take the preliminary breath test will be arrested by the Traffic Police and required to take the second test.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the motorist also refuses to take the second test, he will be liable for the offences of: failure to provide specimen for the preliminary breath test; and failure to provide a specimen for the second test, which has an equivalent penalty to the offence of Driving Under Influence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would also like to assure Mr Murali Pillai that the Traffic Police are now able to conduct the second test on the spot with the mobile Breath Evidential Analyser.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked if there would be a difference in the way disqualification periods operate for the offences of Dangerous and Careless Driving.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There will be no difference in the way disqualification periods operate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Court will have the discretion to depart from the minimum stipulated periods, if there are special reasons to do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Christopher de Souza also asked about the illegal speed trials and the alignment with the penalties for Dangerous and Careless Driving offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Motorists who drive in a dangerous or careless manner will be liable for the offence of Dangerous or Careless Driving whether or not they are involved in an illegal speed trial.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Motorists who partake in illegal street racing will be liable for the offence of Illegal Speed Trial, even if they were not driving dangerously or carelessly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked if community sentencing options, such as Community Work Orders, apply to the RTA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Community Work Orders are meant for reparation and restoration and are only limited to a prescribed list of offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, we do have rehabilitative measures, before an accident even occurs, to help encourage safe driving behaviours by motorists.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, motorists who have clocked a number of demerit points may choose to attend the Safe Driving Course, which helps them learn and practise safe driving habits.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Murali Pillai had also asked if short detention orders can apply to RTA offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One example is the offence of Careless Driving as well as first-time Driving Under Influence offenders.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, let me address the questions on compounded offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng highlighted that some individuals could have compounded an offence without intending to admit guilt.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He asked if composition offences in the RTA amount to an acquittal.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A person who is charged in Court and appeals may be offered composition.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In such instances, once the charge is withdrawn via a discharge amounting to an acquittal, the composition amounts to an acquittal.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, the current case law states that past composition can be treated as an aggravating factor.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It does not matter how the composition came about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Courts should be able to consider an individual’s history of past compounded offences, for example, whether he had one or many past compositions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In any case, this will only apply within the RTA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Mr Louis Ng mentioned in his speech, this is in line with the decisions made by the High Court that compounded offences in RTA may be taken into account for sentencing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Moving forward, people who choose to accept composition should do so with the awareness that the composition could be treated as an aggravating factor in a future conviction.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To be fair to them, due warning will be given at the point the composition is offered.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked about the practical differences between a composition and conviction under RTA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To chart the way forward, several Ministries and stakeholders must work together to tackle the issues from different angles.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Ms Anthea Ong spoke on the need to ensure riders behave responsibly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MHA and the Traffic Police work closely with MOT and LTA to dovetail our road safety and active mobility policies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We already regulate the use of active mobility devices through a comprehensive set of measures.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At this stage of development, the measures cannot be static.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, as Ms Anthea Ong reminds us, an outright ban may be too blunt an act to take because the elderly and the differently-abled have benefited from the use of active mobility devices and so, therefore, it is probably better that the measures be continually updated and improved upon.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This Bill does not focus on active mobility devices and, in any case, MOT oversees this area.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will, therefore, speak more on the approach taken on the road safety front.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On the roads, there have been rules on the use of active mobility devices, such as bicycles.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In February this year, the Government introduced new rules, including the mandatory use of helmets by cyclists on roads.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Now, active mobility users at pedestrian crossings must also "stop and look" before crossing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In April 2019, MHA and the Traffic Police increased the composition sums for cyclist offences on the roads.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have also ramped up public education to raise awareness among active mobility users.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Examples of such measures include the Traffic Police's "Use Your RoadSense" campaign and LTA’s "Safer Together" campaign.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Anthea Ong spoke on the need to ensure that AVs are deployed safely.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Indeed, self-driving technology has the potential to radically transform our transport system and improve our living environment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But we must ensure technology implementation does not endanger human lives.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MHA and the Traffic Police are working closely with MOT to ensure that the AV testing regime is rigorous and the deployment of AVs is done in a cautious and safe manner, taking into account the impact on other road users, including the elderly and differently-abled.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Likewise, we will continue to evaluate different technologies as they are made available.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, like AVs, these different technologies are probably on trial already one way or another.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, let me reassure Members if the technologies improve road safety and are feasible to implement, we will find ways to promote their adoption.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If I may quote Mr Ang Hin Kee, he says: "Beyond the law, I believe we can channel our efforts to cultivate responsible road users and for everybody to have a safer commute." Indeed, we all have a shared responsibility for road safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Yet, this may also be where we most fall short.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah had asked about the underlying causes of unsafe and discourteous road behaviours.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, the Traffic Police recently conducted a nationwide study involving different road user groups.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, this is the situation that we have to deal with.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The findings tell us that we have some way to go before the culture of responsible and gracious road use takes root among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu felt this way, too, and this is why the Traffic Police's effort has always gone beyond enforcement measures to encouraging a safe road use cultural change through engagement, education and, of course, also infrastructural improvements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is also advocated by Members like Mr Melvin Yong and Ms Joan Pereira.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I mentioned in my earlier speech, the Traffic Police and LTA’s recent road safety efforts have shown encouraging results.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira had also, of course, cited some very useful statistics to compare how we fare relative to other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, there is still a need for continual review and improvement, and this Bill is another step in this direction.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Chairman, I beg to move the amendment* standing in the name of the Minister for Home Affairs, as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The consequential amendment* to be made will be made.
